name: Chloe Novak

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Chloe, 43, and I run a loader at the large mine outside our town. I check tyres and the hydraulic lines before dawn, then spend most of the shift moving rock to the crusher; a clean handover to the next operator is the part I like. Sitting in the cab is hard on my back, and the late rota changes wear me down more than the dust. My partner Lena works at a care home, and we have two children in school and a mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew the loaders still need drivers, however clever the office screens get. A quicker parts list might spare us a late finish, and I wouldn't argue with that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't think hype pays the mortgage, and mine still has to come out of the ground. The mine cut overtime last spring, though, and less than a month's bills in our account leaves me watching every shift notice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my loader shifts and ask the foreman for the next month's rota every Friday. When the first year of this small change comes, I'd stop buying lunches at the pit canteen and put that money against the mortgage buffer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm already tight in the chest when hours dip, even if the machines stay ordinary. My son needs new school shoes, and the canteen money is easier to lose than that purchase.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill tells you first that a shift has been lost?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The mortgage debit lands on the third, before my partner Lena's care-home wages reach us. I moved the electricity payment once last spring, and I hated making that call.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the small AI change affect what you do in the cab?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only the parts list, as far as I can see. I still judge the load by sight and listen for the engine, because the rock does not move itself.

say: I would tell the crew **loaders need drivers** even if the office gets faster.
I would welcome **quicker parts lists** if they shorten a late shift.
think: I believe the **mortgage** depends on steady shifts, not claims about AI.
I still worry because our **savings** cover less than one month.
do: Keep **loader shifts** and request the next rota each Friday.
Cut **canteen lunches** and put the difference toward the mortgage buffer.
feel: **Tense** about hours despite little AI change.
S0.quote: I don't think hype pays the mortgage, and mine still has to come out of the ground.
fieldNote: Chloe treats the **loader** as reliable work but remembers last spring’s lost overtime.
The **mortgage debit** comes before Lena’s wages, making even a mild scenario feel financially uncertain.

steps.text: Keep loader shifts and ask the foreman for Friday rotas
Stop pit canteen lunches and build the mortgage buffer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say the office can use smart software for orders, but a screen cannot clear a rockfall. I'd also say managers should explain whose hours change before putting another system in the control room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The first cuts might be planners and clerks, not my loader seat. But if parts ordering gets leaner and production targets rise, our overtime could vanish again; Lena's care-home hours also swing when budgets tighten.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the foreman at the next safety meeting whether the new dispatch software changes our shifts. I'd keep driving and cut the children's weekend takeaway; in the first year of changed schedules, I'd put any overtime into a separate bill account instead of spending it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel cross that the people who choose these systems can call them efficient while we count dinners. I'm not sure the loader job goes in this picture, but the hours could easily get thinner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask if the foreman said nobody was losing a job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask whether the four vacant operator slots are still being filled. Last time a vacancy stayed open, the rest of us covered the shifts for two months without a clear answer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try the dispatch tool yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would use it if the foreman required it, but I would want someone to show me on a real shift. I have never used an AI tool, and I do not learn from a glossy screen in a training room.

say: I would say **software** can handle orders while operators still clear rockfalls.
I would ask managers to explain **hours** before changing dispatch.
think: I suspect **overtime** could disappear even if my loader seat stays.
I worry Lena’s **care-home hours** could also swing.
do: Ask the **foreman** whether dispatch software changes shifts.
Put **overtime pay** in a separate bill account.
Cut the children’s **weekend takeaway** if schedules thin.
feel: **Angry** at decisions made without household costs in view.
S1.quote: Last time a vacancy stayed open, the rest of us covered the shifts for two months without a clear answer.
fieldNote: Chloe separates **operator work** from the office tasks named on the card.
Her concern centers on **unfilled vacancies** and overtime, with Lena’s variable wages compounding a thin cushion.

steps.text: Ask the foreman whether dispatch software changes loader shifts
Put any overtime pay into a separate bill account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew full thinking AI by 2028 could run the planning desk, but we'd still be in the cabs until robots arrived around 2031. I would want the mine to tell us the dates plainly, not send a cheerful poster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is barely enough to clear a small debt, let alone the mortgage. If machines can work the loader in 2031, I expect the company to drop many of our shifts, and there are few mines near us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'd ask the union steward to put robot job numbers on the next meeting agenda, and I'd pay off the store card before replacing our sofa. In 2029, the first year after thinking AI arrives, I'd still run the loader and apply for the maintenance assistant opening at the mine if it comes up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The speed scares me because our pay is already lower than the other operators' pay. I would lie awake over how to keep both children in the same school if I had to chase a job elsewhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a maintenance role really be open to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know; the mine has only advertised one in the last year. I have a vocational certificate and can spot a failing hydraulic line, but I wouldn't claim I can repair the whole fleet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Lena at home tonight?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my partner Lena that the store card has to go before we buy anything for the house. She'd probably ask why I'm suddenly ready to attend a union meeting, and I'd say the robot date makes silence expensive.

say: I would say **thinking AI** threatens planning first, with loader robots around 2031.
I would ask for **plain dates** and likely job numbers.
think: I expect **loader shifts** to fall sharply when robots arrive.
I cannot cover the **mortgage** through a long job search nearby.
do: Ask the **union steward** for robot job numbers this month.
Pay off the **store card** before buying a sofa.
Apply for a mine **maintenance assistant** opening in 2029 if advertised.
feel: **Frightened** about a quick loss of work and school disruption.
S2.quote: I would lie awake over how to keep both children in the same school if I had to chase a job elsewhere.
fieldNote: Chloe understands the **three-year gap** between thinking AI and loader robots.
Her one plausible internal opening is **uncertain**, while mortgage and school ties make relocation costly.

steps.text: Ask union steward to raise robot job numbers at the next meeting
Pay off the store card before replacing the sofa
Apply for a mine maintenance assistant opening in 2029 if advertised

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years to thinking AI gives the planning desk more warning, and our loaders might have until about 2034. The company should use that time for real apprenticeships, with paid places for people already on shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could get my children further through school before robots take the cabs, but I won't pretend eight years clears our mortgage. I trust a paid workshop path more than a vague promise that everyone can become a computer specialist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask payroll this winter for the exact mortgage deduction dates and set a small automatic transfer on each payday. If the mine offered a paid mechanical apprenticeship, I'd enrol; in 2032, after thinking AI arrives, I'd keep driving and ask maintenance whether those places actually exist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel steadier with a few years to organise, but I still count the pay packets. The thought of starting again in my fifties makes me stubborn, then worried about being stubborn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the apprenticeship possible at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would have to keep most of my wage while I learned. My partner Lena can cover a school pickup, but her care-home pay cannot carry the mortgage on its own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the mine offers only unpaid courses?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would leave the course to someone who can afford it. We have less than a month of expenses put aside, so a missed wage is not a theory for us.

say: I would call for **paid apprenticeships** before loader robots arrive around 2034.
I would say the **planning desk** faces change earlier.
think: I trust a **workshop path** more than promises about computer jobs.
I know eight years will not clear our **mortgage**.
do: Set a small **payday transfer** after checking mortgage dates.
Enrol in a **paid mechanical apprenticeship** if the mine offers one.
Keep **driving loaders** through 2032 while checking maintenance places.
feel: **Steadier**, but worried about starting over in my fifties.
S3.quote: I trust a paid workshop path more than a vague promise that everyone can become a computer specialist.
fieldNote: Chloe’s **conditional retraining** requires wage continuity because Lena cannot carry the mortgage alone.
The longer runway softens her response, though she still expects **robot pressure** on operating shifts.

steps.text: Set a small payday transfer after checking mortgage dates
Enrol in a paid mechanical apprenticeship if the mine offers one
Keep driving loaders through 2032 and check maintenance openings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew ten years before full thinking AI is useful time, and robots around 2039 might come when I'm 56. I still wouldn't sign away operator jobs on a promise that new work will appear somewhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 53 when thinking AI arrives, I might have a more manageable mortgage, but I cannot count on that today. At 56, I would still need wages; I have no pension figure that lets me call retirement a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay on the loader and ask the mine's pension office for an actual statement this year. I'd add a fixed amount to the bill account whenever we get a full rota, and in 2037 I'd check whether the mine still needs operators or has paid mechanical places before making a move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A decade gives me room to breathe, even though the end of driving work still bothers me. I am more annoyed by confident speeches about retirement than by the machines themselves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would change your decision in 2037?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A written offer for paid training would change it, or a proper number from the pension office. Without either, I'll keep taking shifts because the mortgage company takes cash, not promises.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would your children figure in the longer plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They will be grown by 2039, and I hope they have work of their own by then. I would still help if I could, but I would not budget as if we still paid for school uniforms.

say: I would say **2039 robots** still threaten operator work at age 56.
I would reject promises of **unspecified jobs** elsewhere.
think: I may have a smaller **mortgage** by 2036, but that is uncertain.
I still need **wages** at 56 without a reliable pension figure.
do: Add money to the **bill account** after full rotas.
Check **operator vacancies** and paid mechanical places in 2037.
feel: **Relieved** by time, though still bothered by the end of driving work.
S4.quote: At 56, I would still need wages; I have no pension figure that lets me call retirement a plan.
fieldNote: The **ten-year runway** permits information gathering without assuming Chloe can retire.
Her plan remains tied to **full rotas** and a written training offer, which neither the card nor employer guarantees.

steps.text: Request an actual pension statement from the mine this year
Add a fixed sum to the bill account after each full rota
Check operator vacancies and paid mechanical places in 2037

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because I can see 2031 arriving before the store card is cleared. A firm date for robot plans, paid mechanical places, and a way to keep wages during training would help. I can't move two school children on a guess about work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who gets the first choice of training places. If managers give them only to the youngest, people like me will be told to adjust after the chance has passed.

headlineQuote: Without either, I'll keep taking shifts because the mortgage company takes cash, not promises.
portrait: Chloe is a **43-year-old loader operator** with two school-age children, a mortgage and less than one month saved.
She trusts **hands-on skill** but is wary of promises about new technology and unnamed replacement jobs.
She sees **planning work** changing before cabs, then worries about robot-led losses in operating shifts.
She would accept **paid mechanical training** if it preserved enough wages for the household.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** gives Chloe too little time before loader robots arrive around 2031.
whatWouldHelp: **Written robot dates** and paid mechanical places with continued wages would help her plan.
